questions.stem: A diode is placed in a circuit. Current flows when connected one way but not the other. This means a diode:

options.text: Has zero resistance in both directions
Only allows current to flow in one direction (forward bias)
Doubles the voltage in the circuit
Stores electrical energy like a battery

questions.explanation: A diode allows current to flow in only one direction — when forward biased (connected the 'right' way). In reverse bias, the diode has very high resistance and blocks current. This makes diodes useful for converting AC to DC (rectification). Option A is wrong — a diode has very high resistance in reverse bias. A diode does not store energy (option D) — that describes a capacitor or battery.

questions.stem: An LED (light-emitting diode) in a circuit must have a resistor connected in series with it. Why?

options.text: To make the LED brighter
To increase the current through the LED
To limit the current flowing through the LED and prevent it from being damaged
To convert AC to DC for the LED

questions.explanation: LEDs have a very low resistance when forward biased. Without a series resistor to limit the current, too much current would flow, overheating and destroying the LED. The resistor drops some of the voltage, keeping the current at a safe level. Options A and B are wrong — the resistor actually reduces brightness and current, which is the whole point.

questions.stem: A variable resistor is connected in series with a motor. When the resistance of the variable resistor is increased, what happens to the motor?

options.text: The motor speeds up because more energy is available
The motor slows down because less current flows through the circuit
The motor reverses direction
Nothing changes — variable resistors only affect voltage

questions.explanation: Increasing the resistance in series increases the total circuit resistance, which reduces the current (from V = IR). Less current through the motor means less power and the motor slows down. This is how speed controllers work — by varying the resistance. Option A is wrong because more resistance means less current and less power delivered to the motor.

questions.stem: A fuse rated at 3 A is connected in a circuit. The current through the circuit increases to 4 A. What happens?

options.text: The fuse allows 3 A through and blocks the extra 1 A
The fuse wire melts, breaking the circuit and stopping all current flow
The fuse increases its resistance to reduce the current to 3 A
The fuse stores the excess charge

questions.explanation: When the current exceeds the fuse rating (3 A), the thin fuse wire heats up due to the excess current (P = I squared x R), melts, and breaks the circuit. This stops ALL current flow, protecting the appliance and wiring from damage or fire. A fuse does not regulate current (options A and C) — it is a safety cut-off device that must be replaced after blowing.

questions.stem: A circuit contains a 12 V battery, a switch, a 6 ohm resistor, and an ammeter all connected in series. When the switch is closed, what reading does the ammeter show?

options.text: 2 A

questions.explanation: Using I = V/R = 12/6 = 2 A. The ammeter and switch have negligible resistance, so the full 12 V acts across the 6 ohm resistor. Option A (72) multiplies V x R. Option B (0.5) divides R by V. Option C (18) adds V and R. This is a straightforward application of Ohm's law.
